stem: An insurer automates renewal risk-tier decisions across 40,000 policies a year. Underwriting has already signed off that 12-month loss ratio is the only measure of correctness, and it won't resolve for a year. Which interim signal should the team report?

opts.t: Track the model's agreement rate against the labeled dataset used to build the risk-tier model.
Escalate every risk-tier call to a licensed underwriter for sign-off until the loss ratio matures.
Track the underwriter override rate on the model's risk-tier calls as the interim signal.
Hold off on any interim signal and report the loss ratio once it matures.

whyRight: Override rate is the fastest available signal that actually tracks the outcome: underwriters override tiers they judge wrong, and persistent overrides predict where the 12-month loss ratio will eventually diverge, unlike a proxy that only resembles a correctness measure.

whyWrong.A: Agreement with the model's own training labels only confirms consistency with past labeling, not whether tiers predict real losses, which the stated business decision requires.
whyWrong.B: No regulatory or licensing requirement is stated; escalating for sign-off is the right response to a regulated decision, not to a problem about which interim signal to report.
whyWrong.D: Waiting a full year discards the interim signal the business needs; long feedback latency calls for a fast surrogate, not silence until the true measure resolves.

t1Clause: 12-month loss ratio ... won't resolve for a year
lessonKey: calls interim model override rate risk s signal tier track underwriter

stem: A downstream router already validates the model's JSON output against a schema with an explicit confidence field, in code, at 200,000 calls a day. A vendor proposes adding a second LLM pass to re-check each response. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Add the LLM pass in parallel, using its verdict to flag low-confidence outputs for review.
Replace the schema validation with the LLM pass, since a model reviews output more flexibly than fixed rules.
Add an explicit confidence field to the JSON schema so the router can flag uncertain outputs.
Keep the existing schema check as the sole gate and decline to add the LLM pass.

whyRight: The schema check already validates output shape and confidence deterministically in code, at full volume, with no false positives from language-model judgment; an added LLM pass tests nothing the existing gate leaves unchecked, only cost and latency.

whyWrong.A: The schema check is already complete and deterministic; layering an LLM review over a working code-level gate adds cost and latency for no coverage the schema doesn't already provide.
whyWrong.B: Replacing a deterministic, working check with a probabilistic model call trades a reliable gate for a costlier, less consistent one, on a requirement the code already satisfies fully.
whyWrong.C: The schema described in the stem already carries the confidence field; this option re-adds something already present, which is correct only when the field is genuinely missing.

t1Clause: already validates the model's JSON output against a schema with an explicit confidence field
lessonKey: add check decline existing gate keep llm pass schema sole

stem: A fraud-investigation workflow processes 3,000 flagged transactions a month. The number of checks needed per case is not known in advance, and each next check depends on what the previous one uncovers. Which architecture should the team implement?

opts.t: A fixed workflow with a predetermined sequence of checks covering the most common fraud patterns.
A coordinator with several specialist subagents dividing the checks by fraud type.
A single retrieval-augmented call that pulls full case history before producing a verdict.
An agent that plans its next check based on what the previous check found.

whyRight: The sequence of checks cannot be listed in advance because each next action depends on what the previous check discovers; that non-enumerable path is exactly the requirement that funds moving to an agent, at 3,000 cases a month.

whyWrong.A: A predetermined sequence only covers cases that follow the common pattern; it silently drops the cases whose next check depends on what an earlier one actually found.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the requirement calls for parallel branches, isolated context, or separated tool privileges; splitting checks across subagents adds coordination cost the task never asked for.
whyWrong.C: Retrieval solves a missing-data problem, not a sequencing problem; the case history doesn't tell the system which check to run next once earlier findings change the path.

t1Clause: each next check depends on what the previous one uncovers

stem: In a hub-and-spoke system, content and metadata must stay distinguishable as subagents hand off findings. Compliance requires every claim traceable to a source, but citations are wrong or missing, though subagents found the right sources. Which two changes fix this? Select two.

opts.t: Have each search subagent return findings as structured records, with source metadata as a separate field.
Have the coordinator pass those structured records to synthesis unmodified, instead of flattening them into text first.
Instruct the synthesis subagent to always cite its sources for every claim it makes.
Widen the coordinator's decomposition so each subagent's slice of the research space is broader.

whyRight: Citations break when content and its source metadata are merged into free text before synthesis; returning structured content-plus-metadata records and preserving that structure through the handoff both fix the root cause the compliance requirement depends on.

whyWrong.C: The synthesis subagent cannot cite metadata it never received as a distinguishable field; an instruction to cite more carefully cannot recover attribution the merge already destroyed.
whyWrong.D: Every subagent already found the right sources here; widening decomposition fixes missing subtopics, not a citation failure caused by how content and metadata were passed downstream.

lessonKey: content free merged metadata passed text were

stem: A product-launch risk review must independently judge data-privacy exposure, marketing-claims risk, and contractual liability, each demanding open-ended synthesis, not a checklist. Legal requires a separate sign-off per dimension, but one prompt currently produces a single combined memo. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Route straightforward launches through a single lighter pass, reserving full decomposition for the hardest cases.
Decompose into three named steps, one per dimension, each evaluated on its own criterion, then integrate for sign-off.
Move to a higher-capability model with a larger context window to handle all three dimensions in one pass.
Split the review into a separate step for every individual clause and marketing claim.

whyRight: Each dimension requires independent open-ended judgment, not checklist items, so one unit can't serve three evaluation criteria at once; naming a step per dimension with its own criterion, then integrating, is the finer decomposition the requirement actually needs.

whyWrong.A: No cost pillar or routine/hard population split is stated; every launch needs all three dimensions judged, so tiering by difficulty doesn't address the mixed-criteria problem here.
whyWrong.C: A larger context window still asks one pass to serve three different evaluation criteria at once; attention dilution across mixed judgment persists regardless of model capacity.
whyWrong.D: These dimensions require open-ended synthesis, not enumerable checklist items; splitting per clause fragments the judgment each dimension needs and loses the context a step had to weigh it.

t1Clause: each demanding open-ended synthesis, not a checklist
lessonKey: criterion decompose dimension each evaluated integrate into named off one own per sign steps then three

stem: Finance will fund a project only with a quantified before/after business case, and the proposed system creates a customer-facing capability that did not exist previously, so no per-unit efficiency baseline exists. Which single business case satisfies both constraints?

opts.t: Compute an efficiency ratio using the process's own prior throughput as the baseline.
Present the business case as transformation, the new revenue or capability the system unlocks.
Delay the funding request until the system runs long enough to build its own retrospective baseline.
Show cost savings from routing routine cases through the smallest model that clears the accuracy bar.

whyRight: The capability has no prior process to divide by, so no valid efficiency ratio exists to report; framing the case as transformation, the value newly unlocked, gives finance the quantified case it requires without fabricating a denominator.

whyWrong.A: The stem states the capability did not exist before, so no prior throughput baseline exists; computing a ratio against a baseline that isn't real misstates the case to finance.
whyWrong.C: Delaying leaves finance's current funding gate unmet now, and a retrospective baseline still divides by a process that never existed before this system.
whyWrong.D: Cost savings answer a different question than the one finance is asking; the funding gate needs a business case for a new capability, not a report on model spend.

t1Clause: creates a customer-facing capability that did not exist previously

stem: A team baselined resolution cost at $4.10 per ticket before deploying a triage assistant on 50,000 monthly tickets. A new ticketing platform now reports $2.30, but counts a ticket 'resolved' at the agent's first reply, not customer confirmation. What should the team do first?

opts.t: Report the $2.30 figure to the stakeholder as the assistant's proven efficiency gain this quarter.
Recompute both figures under one consistent definition of 'resolved' before comparing them.
Treat the deployment as a transformation with no efficiency baseline, since none previously existed.
Launch a dashboard tracking weekly resolution-cost trends so future drift is caught automatically.

whyRight: The $4.10 baseline and the $2.30 figure use different definitions of 'resolved,' so they are not comparable yet. Reconciling both under one consistent definition is required before any efficiency claim is defensible, since the section's rule is that value needs a stable before-and-after unit.

whyWrong.A: The stem states the platform's own definition of 'resolved' changed at launch, so the lower figure reflects a redefinition, not a validated efficiency gain.
whyWrong.C: A prior baseline of $4.10 already exists; the transformation argument only applies where no efficiency baseline is available to compare against.
whyWrong.D: Ongoing monitoring catches future drift but does not resolve whether the current $2.30 figure is already a comparable, trustworthy number.

t1Clause: baselined resolution cost at $4.10 per ticket before deploying a triage assistant
lessonKey: before both comparing consistent definition figures one recompute resolved them under

stem: The team's rule: a feedback loop only closes when a correctness signal reaches a destination that changes system behavior. A churn model's true outcome matures 12 months after each call, but releases ship monthly across 200,000 calls. Which action satisfies the rule now?

opts.t: Add a fast proxy signal, such as override or reopen rate, to steer this month's release decision.
Wait for each cohort's full 12-month churn outcome before making any release decision.
Log every prediction and eventual outcome in a dashboard for quarterly leadership review.
Route the outcome signal into the model's retrieval and indexing layer for citations.

whyRight: The rule requires a correctness signal to reach a destination that changes behavior before the next decision, and releases ship monthly while the true outcome takes twelve months to mature. Only a fast proxy — override or reopen rate — can steer this month's release before then.

whyWrong.B: Releases ship monthly, so waiting a full year for the outcome leaves every release decision in between with no correctness signal at all.
whyWrong.C: A dashboard records predictions and outcomes but carries no correctness label that changes what the model or prompt does next.
whyWrong.D: This churn model has no retrieval or citation layer; that fix belongs to a document-retrieval system, not a monthly release cadence.

lessonKey: add alongside fast override proxy rate reopen

stem: A team has selected an agentic design for a document-review task with unlisted scope, and a stated p95 latency commitment of 4 seconds. The agent's mean latency is 2.1 seconds. What should the team do before shipping?

opts.t: Ship the design; a 2.1-second mean latency comfortably clears the 4-second commitment.
Replace the agent with a fixed workflow immediately, since agent latency is inherently unpredictable.
Add a retry-with-timeout wrapper around the agent's slowest tool calls.
Check the agent's tail, p95 latency, against the 4-second commitment before concluding it ships.

whyRight: An SLA is stated in p95 terms, and a 2.1-second mean passing does not confirm the tail clears a 4-second commitment. The rung is filtered by the stated requirement before comparison, so the agent's actual tail distribution must be checked before shipping.

whyWrong.A: The commitment is stated in p95, not mean; a comfortable mean says nothing about whether the tail of the distribution also clears 4 seconds.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the stem shows scope is actually fixed and enumerable; discarding the agent on a latency guess, before checking, is premature.
whyWrong.C: Wrapping slow calls in retries treats a possible SLA miss as already confirmed, without first checking whether the tail actually breaches 4 seconds.

t1Clause: a document-review task with unlisted scope
lessonKey: agent check even fail if may mean passes re s sla tail

stem: A drafting role must never hold write access to case files; a verifier must never hold search access, and must stay uncontaminated by the drafter's own notes. 300 daily cases run under a two-hour SLA. Which two facts justify a multi-agent design? Select two.

opts.t: A latency requirement, since the two-hour SLA is what actually forces the two roles apart.
Direct coordination between the drafter and verifier would resolve disagreements faster than a coordinator can.
Per-role privilege separation — the drafter cannot write, and the verifier cannot search.
Context isolation — the verifier must never see the drafter's own search notes.

whyRight: The stem states two independent facts that each justify splitting roles: the drafter and verifier hold mutually exclusive tool privileges, and the verifier's judgment must stay uncontaminated by the drafter's own notes — privilege separation and context isolation, the two stated justifications.

whyWrong.A: Volume and an SLA are stated, but nothing says the 300 cases must fan out in parallel; the same figures hold under one agent working sequentially.
whyWrong.B: Direct role-to-role channels dissolve the coordinator boundary that buys privilege separation and isolation in the first place, and were never stated as needed.

t1Clause: 300 daily cases run under a two-hour SLA

stem: A monthly audit of 8,000 vendor invoices checks the same five line items, in the same order, every time. The finance director, chasing lower review cost, proposes a dynamic, adaptive agent instead of the fixed pipeline. What should the team do?

opts.t: Adopt the adaptive agent so it can reason about edge cases the fixed template might miss.
Split the audit into confidence tiers, routing unusual invoices to a costlier review path.
Keep the fixed pipeline, but add prompt instructions telling it to work faster.
Keep the fixed pipeline; the review is identical every time, and adaptivity adds cost for nothing.

whyRight: The five line items and their order never vary, so the review is fully predictable and reproducible; per the section's rule, a fixed pipeline is correct here, and an adaptive agent would add nondeterminism and per-call reasoning cost without touching the stated cost goal.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the stem is discovered at runtime; the five items and their order are already fixed, so agentic reasoning adds variance to a solved problem.
whyWrong.B: The stem never states any invoices are harder or unusual; confidence-tier routing answers a difficulty split that isn't present in this uniform review.
whyWrong.C: Faster-sounding instructions don't lower per-invoice cost or change what makes the audit slow; the pipeline itself was never the source of the cost pressure.

t1Clause: checks the same five line items, in the same order, every time
